root_idea.summary: The root centers on strength, solidity, and the resilient outer covering of the body: the skin.
root_idea.development: From the skin's firmness and resistance, the lexicon develops meanings of bodily covering, physical strength and endurance, hard ground, and objects made tough or covered with skin.

qac_form_accounting.reason: Displayed under the normalized Form I perfect citation form.
Displayed as the normalized singular noun جَلْدَة.
The Quranic plural جُلُود is presented under the supported singular citation form جِلْد.

senses.definition: To flog or strike a person with a whip as corporal punishment.
senses.usage_conditions: The Quranic form occurs as a plural imperative in the legal instruction to administer a prescribed flogging.

senses.definition: A lash or stripe of flogging.
senses.usage_conditions: In the Quranic legal construction, the word counts individual lashes or stripes administered in a flogging.

senses.definition: Skin; the body's outer integument, including animal hide.
senses.usage_conditions: The Quran uses the plural جُلُود for the physical skins or hides of human beings and animals, including skins that feel, testify, burn, or are replaced.

senses.definition: The body or embodied self, spoken of through its skins.
senses.usage_conditions: This is a Quranic metonymic use distinguished from the literal skin; in the discussion of 39:23, skins are understood as the bodies, contrasted with hearts as the selves or inner persons.

senses.definition: The pudenda or genitals, by euphemistic metonymy.
senses.usage_conditions: An alternative Quranic interpretation of جُلُود in 41:20–21; the literal interpretation, “skins,” is also reported for these verses.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To hit or hurt the skin, to beat a person, or to strike with a whip or sword.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The Quranic legal flogging is a specialized use of this broader striking action; the passive result of being struck or flogged is also expressed by مَجْلُود.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Of a serpent, to bite; according to another usage, for a specified black serpent, to strike with its tail.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A specialized animal-related usage.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To approach sexually or have sexual intercourse.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A figurative or metonymic use; the related phrase جَلْدُ عُمَيْرَةَ refers to masturbation.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To strike someone against the ground and throw him down prostrate; in the passive, to fall to the ground under an overpowering condition such as sleepiness.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Used in constructions with بِهِ.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To compel someone against his will to do something.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A figurative transitive construction with عَلَى.

other_classical_meanings.definition: In idiomatic passive expressions, to be regarded as possessing every good quality; in a separate reported use, to be suspected or accused of lying.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: These are specialized figurative assessments rather than the physical striking sense.

other_classical_meanings.definition: For land, plants, or people to be affected or smitten by hoarfrost or rime.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A specialized intransitive or passive-like use concerning frost damage or exposure.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To be or become hardy, strong, sturdy, and enduring or patient; the same hardness can describe robust palms and tough, compact dates.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Applied primarily to people and, by extension, to resilient plants or hard, durable produce.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To skin a slaughtered camel or other beast.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: This Form II verb is specially used for removing the skin from a slaughtered camel, where سَلَخَ is said to be less usual.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To cover or clothe something with skin; by extension, to bind or cover a book.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The verb can describe both removing a skin and applying or covering with one, two opposed operations distinguished by context.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To order that someone be flogged.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A reported usage preserved in the lexical record without an authority being specified there.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To render a person hardy, strong, sturdy, and enduring or patient.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A causative Form II use derived from the quality of hardiness.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To contend with someone in fighting, especially in combat with swords.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A reciprocal or adversarial Form III construction.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To constrain or compel someone to have recourse to, or stand in need of, someone or something.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An idiomatic Form IV construction with إِلَى.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To constrain oneself to endure with hardiness and patience, or to affect and display such hardiness.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The verb can mean genuinely bracing oneself or merely putting on a show of strength; it may take عَنْ when it implies enduring the loss or absence of something.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To drink all that is in a vessel.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A specialized Form VIII usage applied to consuming the vessel's entire contents.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A strong, hardy, or swift she-camel; in related livestock terminology, a ewe, she-goat, or she-camel characterized by a specified condition of offspring or milk, including abundant, scant, or absent milk.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The terminology varies by animal and authority; some usages emphasize strength for labor, while others classify females without young or milk.

other_classical_meanings.definition: The body and limbs, the whole person, or the person himself.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A metonymy based on the body being enclosed by skin; the cited lexical form is the plural أَجْلَاد.

other_classical_meanings.definition: The stripped skin of one young animal used to clothe or simulate another young animal, or a stuffed skin placed before a female so that she accepts and suckles a non-offspring.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A pastoral practice involving the transfer or simulation of an animal's scent and appearance.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Hard ground, including hard and level or level but rough terrain.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Used adjectivally of land or a place.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A piece or portion of skin.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A more specific term than جِلْد.

other_classical_meanings.definition: The eyelid.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An anatomical specialization of the term for a piece or layer of skin.

other_classical_meanings.definition: One's own people, company, or kinsfolk.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A figurative expression for people of the same stock or group.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A woman who has been flogged with a whip.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A specialized nominal use distinct from the ordinary passive description of someone beaten.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Congealed or frozen water; ice.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A related but distinct cold-weather noun, alongside the meaning hoarfrost or rime.

other_classical_meanings.definition: One of the layers or coats of the eye.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A diminutive anatomical term derived from جِلْدَة.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A dealer in skins.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A relational noun derived from جُلُود, the plural of جِلْد.

other_classical_meanings.definition: An official whose occupation is flogging others with a whip; more generally, an executioner.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The broader executioner sense is a later or extended usage noted in the lexical record.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A piece of skin held by a wailing woman and used to slap her face or cheek during mourning.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A ritual mourning implement; مِجْلَاد is given as a related form.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Covered with skin; hence covered or bound as a book, and a bound volume.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The nominal extension from skin-covering to a book or volume is conventional.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A bone covered only by skin, with nothing remaining on it but the skin.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A specialized descriptive use.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A horse that is hardy and not frightened or impatient when beaten with a whip.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A figurative application of endurance under beating.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A fixed quantity of a load, traditionally six hundred pounds in weight.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A technical measure of burden or weight.

other_classical_meanings.definition: One who binds books or covers them with skin.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An occupational noun derived from the Form II skin-covering verb.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Having been struck or hurt in the skin; beaten or flogged.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A passive participial result of the striking and flogging branch of جَلَدَ.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A place where people contend in fighting with swords.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A place noun derived from the Form VIII fighting usage.

cautions: The plural Quranic form جُلُود is normalized under the singular dictionary headword جِلْد.
The interpretation of جُلُود in 41:20–21 is genuinely variant: literal skins and euphemistic reference to the pudenda are both preserved.
